entry.title: Show HN: Pots - Open-source Grok Bot alternative, used by 6 startups for a month (Source: hnrss.org | Category: Hacker News)
entry.summary: Hi HN, I'm Crokily. Pots is an AI coworker that lives in the chat your team already uses: Slack, Discord, Telegram, or any channel with a Chat SDK adapter. It is MIT-licensed and runs on a machine you give it, with the model you choose. To be honest, the first time I used Grok Bot, its design really impressed me. Unlike OpenClaw before it, it was not just Claude Code connected to a chat app. It truly cared about how it works with people. It felt like a living AI assistant, and working with it was painless. That is the idea I kept learning from the whole time I built Pots: it is not an agent hooked up to a chat channel. It should be a coworker that feels alive and is comfortable to work with. But Grok Bot is only Grok's bot. Which model you get depends on your X subscription, your data and your machine are all in the cloud, and most of all, it is a standalone app, and most of its features serve that app. Pots is a bit different. In Sydney I have talked with quite a few founders. Grok Bot is good, and it helps them a lot with their personal tasks. But when I asked who had actually put Grok Bot into their company's work to make their startup team faster, nobody had. So I think Pots is in a different place from Grok Bot, and from most open-source Grok Bot alternatives: it grew out of what real startup teams need. Before I open-sourced it, 6 small startups I met at startup events had been using it with me for over a month. Pots is built first for the channels startup teams already work in, not for an app of its own, so most of what it does serves the places where you actually work. The teams use Pots as a middle layer: a CEO talks ideas through with the team in chat, Pots listens, and then it builds a prototype that both sides can check. They use Pots for competitor research: because Pots runs inside their channels, it knows their product well. Not only the GitHub repo, but the team's daily discussions and what the team cares about. Pots has been listening quietly the whole time, so it knows the product with no setup at all. It also works well with each channel: it talks to people with the channel's own controls, like Slack and Discord buttons and cards, and when it hands over something complex, it deploys a page with its built-in server so everyone sees it in a better form. So Pots is different from Grok Bot and from most open-source alternatives. It came out of what real startup teams need. Its channel features start from what each company's work needs, and it can join your real work setup with no setup and still do well, instead of being one more app that nobody uses and that is hard to start with. And it ran in real business for a while before I cleaned it up and open-sourced it. The difference from Grok Bot is also exactly why I made Pots an open-source Grok Bot alternative. I have OpenAI and Claude subscriptions with plenty of quota, and my own servers, so I don't want an X subscription to limit me. I want to use whatever model I want and do whatever I want. I can even switch to an open model, and none of my data goes into anyone's pocket. Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50452040 Points: 1 # Comments: 0

entry.title: Show HN: Ember.js, Re-Born in Rust (Source: hnrss.org | Category: Hacker News)
entry.summary: 7 years ago I began migrating all my back-ends to Rust. Front-ends, however, remained an issue. As an Ember developer for 15 years, I've been a big fan of MVC, and keeping code out of templates. Ember's HTMLbars syntax has been the thing I've leaned on to keep my templates clean and maintainable, so that I could stay focused and organized. But the JS/TS toolchains were always a point of friction. As I worked on new Rust back-ends, while maintaining old Ember front-ends, I dreamed of rewriting those Ember routes, controllers, models, and adapters in type-safe idiomatic Rust. The Leptos creator Greg Johnston finally gave me a nudge to get something going. So after 3 years of planning, and 4 months of execution, the Auric framework is ready for public eyes. It's Ember.js, re-imagined in Rust (and not just an AI port). It stays faithful to Ember, HTMLbars, and Ember Data, while leveraging Leptos to realize all of the reactive concerns (which implies Trunk for WASM packaging, and full SSR support). It's open source on GitLab at: https://gitlab.com/megalithic-llc/auric-spa The sample app is the Auric website itself, which contains demo pages for all of ember-bootstrap, ember-power-select, and ember-concurrency add-ons, re-imagined in pure idiomatic Rust, backed by Actix Web based SSR. Templates and components are at /src/templates/ and /src/components/, while their code-generated Leptos counterparts are at /src/generated/views/ and /src/generated/components/. Templates are up to 7x smaller than the Leptos views derived from them, thanks to the timeless elegance of HTMLbars. That seems like an important data point, now that our coding assistants threaten to automate us out of love with our webapps, by turning them into something we no longer enjoy looking at. The longer back-story was published to Medium a few days ago: https://medium.com/@david_77274/ember-js-devs-welcome-to-the... entry.title: Show HN: Black Ops II statically recompiled to native ARM64 macOS (Source: hnrss.org | Category: Hacker News)
entry.summary: I grew up with Black Ops 2 and wanted to see if I could make it work on my 2020 MacBook Pro. So I used Claude Opus 5.5 to create a tool that converts your copy of the game (from Steam) to a native ARM64 Mac app, with almost 60fps in all areas. The whole game is statically recompilated ahead-of-time (AOT) and does not use any emulator whatsoever, be it Wine, Crossover or Rosetta. The best thing is the performance, although some heat issues are still to fix. You get to play the whole Campaign, local Multiplayer (with bots) and local Zombies (all DLCs maps; you need to have them in your Steam library obviously) at about 60fps. Split-screen was not in the PC version, but I've been working on it lately; it's coming soon! LAN mode is on the roadmap for later too :) Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50449891 Points: 30 # Comments: 2

entry.title: Show HN: Get your coding agent off ~2019 JavaScript, onto modern web primitives (Source: hnrss.org | Category: Hacker News)
entry.summary: Browsers natively handle a lot of what used to take 50 lines of JS (or a dependency): `CSS.highlights` for text range highlighting without s everywhere, `` and showModal() give you backdrops and ideal focus management, `field-sizing` to auto-grow textareas as the user types.. (Something yesterday's ftrain post touched on [0]) Models know about some of these by name, but consistently won't default to using the platform-native solution and instead prefer the incumbent +JS based pattern. We started an effort in Chrome to supplement coding agents with this key domain knowledge and we're shipping our 1.0 today, in collaboration with Firefox, MDN, and Edge. 200+ guides (~1.7MB) of curated, hand-crafted implementation best-practices from web experts, updated as the web evolves. (Open source, obv, so.. we'll welcome your bikeshedding ;) Readable versions here: [1] I've spent the last 9 months obsessing over how to ship this as an agent skill + (Agentic RAG) CLI without blowing up your context window. (Or cedeing activation mechanics to MCP dynamic tool search). The skill description is minmaxed for activating on relevant frontend tasks. The RAG work I'm pretty proud of... originally a 500mb native stack down to a ~7MB pure-JS package, ~10ms search on your CPU. We just introduced a deterministic 'legacy-scan' (trained on 30k github repos) to identify old 'n dusted patterns that your agent can modernize. (92% avg precision on held-out repos.) People make a lot of claims about what coding agents are good/bad at. We wanted receipts, so we invested heavily in eval infra [2] to help us hill-climb, but also to identify when knowledge is common enough we can prune our guides. (Ofc, some of the things we thought AI didn't know turned out to be wrong :) We run codex/claude/agy against 200 tasks without the skill and then with.. In total ~1,700 playwright/AST-based assertions. Agents go from 55% pass unguided to 92% guided. Try it out: DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1 npx modern-web-guidance@latest install DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1 npx modern-web-guidance@latest search "animate dialog modal" DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1 npx modern-web-guidance@latest legacy-scan ./src If you spot something wrong or weird, give us a holler! Longer write-up on the 1.0: https://developer.chrome.com/blog/modern-web-guidance-v1 --- 0: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50416456 1: https://developer.chrome.com/docs/modern-web-guidance/guides 2: https://googlechrome.github.io/modern-web-guidance-src/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50443812 Points: 376 # Comments: 118
